one_liner: Research static RV32-to-x86/ARM binary translator built on LLVM; translated MiBench runs near native, far ahead of QEMU and rv8.
what_it_does: Takes RISC-V RV32G relocatable object files (the translator's positional arguments are '<input object files>'), lifts every function to LLVM IR, optimizes it with opt -O3 and lowers it with llc to 32-bit x86 (AVX) or ARM, then links it with a small runtime. Calls to undefined symbols are bound to a fixed whitelist of about 80 host libc/libm functions (sbt/libc.c), syscalls go through a runtime handler, and indirect calls go through a generated dispatcher over known functions. It is a build pipeline (scripts/auto and mibench/genmake.py generate Makefiles), not an emulator you point at an arbitrary linked binary.
how_it_is_fast: Ahead-of-time whole-program translation removes the run-time costs a dynamic translator pays (decode, translation, code-cache lookup, dispatch), and LLVM's -O3 pipeline re-optimizes the lifted code. The register mapping mode matters most: 'globals' keeps guest registers in global variables (2-15x slower than native on several programs), 'locals' gives each function a local register file that LLVM can promote to host registers and syncs it at calls, and 'abi' syncs only the registers the RISC-V calling convention makes live across calls and returns, which yields the best numbers. libc and libm calls run as native host code.
when_to_use: Research on RISC-V emulation quality: it gives an upper bound for what a translator can reach (committed CSVs: 1.02-1.08x native on x86 with 'abi' mapping, 1.16x on ARM) to compare a DBT design against.
Running RV32 programs you build yourself (gcc -O3 objects, single-threaded, ABI-conformant C) on a 32-bit x86 or ARM Linux host when you can rebuild them through its toolchain.
Teaching or prototyping LLVM-based binary lifting: the translator is compact C++ (sbt/*.cpp) with debug options such as -commented-asm and -a2s for source-annotated output.
when_not_to_use: Running arbitrary or stripped RISC-V executables, RV64 code, self-modifying or JIT-generating code, or dynamically loaded libraries: it needs relocatable RV32 objects and translates statically; use QEMU, rv8, rv32emu or libriscv instead.

Programs calling libc functions outside the whitelist in sbt/libc.c, external functions with more than 8 parameters (rejected by the translator), or indirect calls to code the dispatcher does not know (aborts with 'FATAL ERROR: at icaller: function not found').

Code that needs exact RISC-V floating-point state: FCSR emulation and fcvt input validation are off by default (-enable-fcsr, -enable-fcvt-validation), and 'abi' mode assumes every function obeys the calling convention.
Anything needing maintenance or a current toolchain: last commit 2019-03-06, built from pinned OpenISA forks of LLVM and clang and a gcc 7.3.0 RISC-V toolchain branch, no issues or releases.
Deep recursion or large stack frames without tuning: the guest stack is a fixed buffer (-stack-size, default 4096 bytes; the MiBench builds pass 16 KB, 128 KB or 1 MB per program).

integration.form: translator CLI (riscv-sbt) plus Python Makefile generator; build from source or Docker image
integration.dependencies: OpenISA forks of LLVM and clang (submodules pinned in docker/commits.txt), OpenISA riscv-gnu-toolchain (gcc-7.3.0 branch), riscv-isa-sim/fesvr/pk, i686 gcc for native comparisons, perf for measurement
integration.min_toolchain: not documented beyond the pinned submodule commits; the Dockerfiles in docker/ are the stated reference
integration.platforms: input RV32G objects (ilp32d hard-float or ilp32 soft-float ABI); output 32-bit x86 Linux (i686, AVX by default, MMX option) or ARM Linux (Thumb)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; translated programs use a single fixed-size guest stack and all measured workloads are single-threaded

gotchas: Like-for-like flaw in the QEMU/rv8 comparison: the SBT binds libc/libm calls to native host libc (sbt/libc.c, Caller::callExternal), while QEMU and rv8 emulate the RISC-V libc too. On the 5 programs where native code spends under 10% of cycles in its own code (stringsearch, basicmath, fft-std, fft-inv, patricia), the SBT's total-time slowdown is 1.03x against QEMU's 9.76x; on the other 14 the gap is still large (SBT abi 1.01x, QEMU 5.19x), so the win holds but is inflated for libc-heavy rows (derived from page data).

The headline 'x' columns (x86-avx-gcchf.csv) multiply wall time by perf's share of cycles in the benchmark's own DSO, so for basicmath (2.77% own code natively) the ratio rests on a few milliseconds of samples; runs are short (0.05-2.4 s, n=10 default) and several translated rows beat native (adpcm-encode 0.70x, bitcount abi 0.77x, dijkstra 0.87x), which reflects gcc -O3 native versus LLVM -O3 re-optimization rather than translation alone.

Paper and repo numbers disagree: the SSCAD 2018 abstract (search snippet only; sol.sbc.org.br is blocked here) reports 12% overhead on x86 and 35% on ARM, while the committed CSVs give 1.08x (abi) and 1.23x (locals) on x86 and 1.16x (abi) and 1.34x (locals) on ARM (derived from page data); no CPU model is stated anywhere reachable.

rv8 and OVP rows cover only 10 of 19 programs (notes/rv8: crashes, wrong results, build failures) and the other 9 are zero-filled placeholders, so their geomean rows (rv8 2.85x, OVP 4.92x) are over a different program set than QEMU's 6.13x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over rv8, rv32emu or libriscv only when you can rebuild the RV32 program and want near-native speed as a research reference; those dynamic translators and interpreters run unmodified binaries, are maintained (rv32emu, libriscv), and handle code this SBT cannot. Instrew is the closer LLVM-based design if you need dynamic translation of real executables.
verified_claims_summary: Committed MiBench result CSVs (19 programs, RV32G built with gcc -O3, translated ahead of time to 32-bit x86 AVX via LLVM; CPU not stated) show the SBT at 1.08x (abi) and 1.23x (locals) of native gcc -O3 i686 time counting only the program's own code, or 1.02x and 1.11x with libc time included, while qemu-riscv32 user mode is 6.13x and rv8 2.85x on the 10 programs it could run (total time, emulating RISC-V libc).
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-03-06 (repo now redirects to lmcad-unicamp/riscv-sbt, no issues filed), MIT-licensed and copyable, but a research prototype tied to 2018-era forked LLVM, clang and gcc 7.3.0 toolchains; expect to rebuild through its Docker setup.
